extracted.intended_audience: neuroscientists, psychologists, psychopharmacologists, and graduate students interested in affective neuroscience and the neural bases of reward and pleasure
extracted.subtask_description: A glossary within a research review that defines core concepts and distinctions used in affective neuroscience and reward research (e.g., liking vs 'liking', wanting vs 'wanting', reward, reinforcement, neural coding vs causation). Intended to reduce terminological confusion in empirical and theoretical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective valence or hedonic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Affective valence is the hedonic niceness or nastiness (‘liking’ versus ‘disliking’) of reward or aversion that is essential to emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hedonic valence is a brain-generated process actively added to a stimulus by specialized neural systems (e.g., accumbens/pallidal hedonic hotspots). It is neither an inherent property of a stimulus nor a mere epiphenomenon. This objective neural–psychological process supports an affective neuroscience of positive affect. The term 'hedonic' is often used for positive pleasures specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Associative Pavlovian or instrumental learning forms links between stimuli or behavioral events; cognitive learning mechanisms form higher-order rule-based predictions, declarative expectations, and goal-directed plans based on experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish basic associative learning (S–R, S–S) from cognitive/declarative learning; learning is one of multiple components contributing to reward alongside 'liking' and 'wanting'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liking (without quotation marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective hedonic reactions — the everyday sense of liking or pleasure, referring most directly to a conscious experience or subjective feeling of niceness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this term for conscious subjective pleasure reports or experiences; it contrasts with objective, behaviorally/neuro-measured hedonic reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Liking' (with quotation marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: An objective hedonic reaction, measured behaviorally or neurally, whether or not accompanied by conscious pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core 'liking' reactions result from activity in identifiable brain systems (hedonic hotspots) and can be measured (e.g., facial expressions to tastes homologous across mammals). In humans, 'liking' reactions may occur unconsciously (objective neural/behavioral signatures without conscious awareness). Use quotes to mark objective, measurable hedonic reactions distinct from subjective feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive hedonic valence, as a 'liking' reaction or subjective liking reaction to the hedonic impact of a stimulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can mean subjective conscious niceness or a more basic core 'liking' reaction generated by hedonic brain systems (conscious pleasure may require additional cognitive awareness mechanisms). Under some conditions objective neural processing of pleasure may occur without conscious awareness (an unconscious 'liking' reaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure, neural causation of
rubrics_metrics.description: A brain mechanism (e.g., a hedonic hotspot) in which neural activation causes an increase in objective 'liking' reactions, or in subjective ratings or experiences of conscious pleasure, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'necessary cause' (region required for normal pleasure; damage reduces pleasure) versus 'sufficient cause' (activation can generate increased pleasure above baseline). Some substrates can be both; others may be sufficient only. Presence of activity does not always imply pleasure (necessary vs sufficient differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure, neural coding of
rubrics_metrics.description: A brain mechanism in which activation correlates highly with the occurrence of pleasure, so that the neural activation is a reliable brain marker for pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neural coding may function as causation but can also arise as consequence rather than cause (e.g., coding activity may reflect downstream processes like complex emotion, memory, cognition). Coding is a broader category than causation and should be considered separately when interpreting neural signals related to pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive reinforcement or reinforcer
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms sometimes used to denote pleasure or a pleasure-causing stimulus, but ambiguous because they have pleasure-free meanings in behaviorist theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behaviorist definitions (Skinner, Hull) define reinforcement as strengthening of responses (S–R stamping-in) or increased operant frequency without positing affective mechanisms. Defining pleasure solely as positive reinforcement is problematic due to empirical double dissociations: pleasure can occur without behavioral reinforcement, and reinforcement can occur without pleasure (e.g., 'wanting' without 'liking' via dopamine manipulations). Therefore grapple directly with pleasure and reward rather than outsourcing to reinforcement terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward
rubrics_metrics.description: A composite psychological process requiring multiple brain systems; a single instance typically contains 'liking', 'wanting', and learning components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brain manipulations can dissociate these components. Each component can occur without conscious awareness (core 'liking', core 'wanting', implicit learning). Conscious experience of reward requires additional cognitive processing and awareness-generating mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wanting (without quotation marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The everyday sense of the word as a subjective desire; conscious wanting typically requires cortical mechanisms that generate declarative goals (based on memory or imagery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for goal-directed, declarative desires where the subject can imagine or plan to obtain something. Distinguish from subcortical incentive processes that do not require declarative representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Wanting' (with quotation marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incentive salience: a motivational process within reward that mirrors hedonic 'liking' and makes stimuli attractive when attributed to them by mesolimbic brain systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incentive salience ('wanting') is strongly influenced by mesolimbic dopamine but is separable from hedonic impact. It can produce irrational desire for things one does not like or expect to like (e.g., drug addiction, false pleasure electrodes). 'Wanting' without 'liking' can arise via incentive sensitization because 'wanting' mechanisms are largely subcortical and separable from cortical declarative expectation and planning.
